cards.s: Branch protection and the PR workflow
cards.html:
Now make CI mandatory. In your repository: Settings → Rules → Rulesets → New branch ruleset. Target the default branch and enable:

  • Restrict deletions and Block force pushes.
  • Require a pull request before merging, with 1 required approval (for a solo portfolio project you can set 0 approvals but still require the PR).
  • Require status checks to pass: add ci-ok. (You could list

lint, test (3.12), test (3.13) and model-gate one by one; the first what-if below shows why one aggregator is better.) A check name only appears in the list after it has run at least once.

  • Require branches to be up to date before merging: the PR must contain the latest main, so CI tested the real combination.

cards.s: Branch protection and the PR workflow
cards.html:
(The older Settings → Branches → Branch protection rules page does the same; rulesets are the newer, more flexible version.)

The full PR workflow, end to end:

terminal:

cards.s: Branch protection and the PR workflow
cards.html:
git switch main && git pull
git switch -c feat/validate-age
# ... edit code and tests ...
uv run pytest && git commit -am "feat: reject applicants under 18"
git push -u origin feat/validate-age
gh pr create --fill               # or open the PR in the browser
gh pr checks --watch              # watch CI from the terminal
# after approval and green checks:
gh pr merge --squash --delete-branch

What if… a required check shows "Expected — Waiting for status to be reported" forever?

What happens: The PR cannot be merged. All runs are green, but one required check stays yellow, and nothing is running.

cards.s: Branch protection and the PR workflow
cards.html: Why: Required checks are matched by name. The matrix creates names such as test (3.12). If you change the matrix to 3.13 and 3.14, the job test (3.12) never runs again, but the ruleset still waits for it. The same happens when a path filter skips the whole workflow or an if: skips a required job (a skipped job counts as passed, but a workflow that never started reports nothing).

cards.s: Branch protection and the PR workflow
cards.html:
What you do: Do not make every matrix job required. Add one small aggregator job that depends on everything and require only that:

  ci-ok:
    if: always()                 # run even if a dependency failed
    needs: [lint, test, model-gate]
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: Fail if any dependency failed or was cancelled
        if: >-
          contains(needs.*.result, 'failure') ||
          contains(needs.*.result, 'cancelled')
        run: exit 1

Now you can change the matrix freely; the ruleset only knows ci-ok. The if: always() is essential: without it, ci-ok would be skipped when a dependency fails, and skipped counts as success.

cards.s: Branch protection and the PR workflow
cards.html:
What if… the team is busy and "require up to date" becomes a race?

What happens: Five PRs are approved. You update yours with main, wait six minutes for CI, and just before you click merge somebody else merges. Your PR is out of date again. Repeat.

Why: "Up to date" guarantees that CI tested the exact combination, but it serialises the team on your attention.

cards.s: Branch protection and the PR workflow
cards.html:
What you do: A merge queue (Rulesets → Require merge queue). You click "Merge when ready"; GitHub builds a temporary branch with main + the PRs ahead of yours + yours, runs CI on it, and merges if it is green. Workflows must listen to the queue's event, or the queue waits forever:

on:
  pull_request:
  merge_group:        # run CI on the merge queue's temporary branch

Sooner or later CI needs credentials: an API key for an LLM, a token for a tracking server. Never put them in the code or the workflow file. GitHub stores them encrypted: Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions.

KindUse forIn a workflow
SecretPasswords, API keys, tokens. Write-only in the UI and masked as *** in logs.${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
VariableNon-secret configuration: region, role ARN, URLs. Visible in the UI.${{ vars.AWS_ROLE_ARN }}
Environment secret/variableValues that differ per environment (staging vs. production) and can be protected by approvals (Level 3).same syntax, inside a job with environment:
GITHUB_TOKENAutomatic, short-lived token for the GitHub API in this repository; scope it with permissions:.${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

Pass secrets to the step that needs them, as environment variables:

using a secret:

      - name: Faithfulness eval
        env:
          ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
        run: uv run python eval/run_eval.py --faithfulness

Watch out: What never to commit, and what to do if you did

Never commit .env files, cloud access keys, private keys, notebook outputs containing credentials, or data with personal information (GDPR! (DSGVO)). Add them to .gitignore before the first commit. If a secret was pushed, deleting the file is not enough: it stays in Git history and bots scan public GitHub within minutes. Revoke and rotate the key immediately, then clean history if needed. GitHub's secret scanning and push protection (free for public repos) block many known key formats on push; turn them on in Settings → Code security.

Secrets are not passed to workflows triggered by pull requests from forks, because anybody could open such a PR and print them. Keep this in mind for open-source projects: expensive or credentialed jobs run on push to main or behind a label set by a maintainer, a pattern you will use for the LLM evaluation in Level 4.

What if… a secret appears in the log in plain text after all?

What happens: Masking replaces the exact secret string with ***. Your step prints it base64-encoded, URL-encoded, or split across two lines, and the transformed value is visible to anyone who can read the logs.

What you do: Never print secrets, not even "to debug". If a step derives a sensitive value (a token fetched at runtime), register it for masking before it is used: echo "::add-mask::$TOKEN". If one leaked: rotate it, then delete the run's logs (run page → … → Delete all logs).

What if… I switch to pull_request_target so fork PRs get secrets?

What happens: It works, and it is one of the most exploited GitHub Actions mistakes ("pwn request").

Why: pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository, with secrets and a write token. If the workflow then checks out and runs the PR's code (ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} followed by pip install or pytest), the stranger's code runs with your secrets. A conftest.py in the PR is enough to send them to the attacker.

What you do: Use pull_request for anything that runs PR code. Use pull_request_target only for tasks that never execute the PR's code (labelling, commenting). For paid evaluations of fork PRs, let a maintainer run them after reading the code.

What if… my Dependabot PRs fail because secrets are empty?

What happens: PRs opened by Dependabot run CI, but every step that uses a secret fails as if the secret did not exist.

Why: For safety, workflows triggered by Dependabot do not receive Actions secrets. They get Dependabot secrets, a separate store (Settings → Secrets and variables → Dependabot).

What you do: Make unit tests independent of secrets (fakes, as in Level 4), and add a Dependabot secret only where a dependency PR truly needs one.

A lock file freezes versions, which is good for reproducibility and bad for security: vulnerabilities in old versions stay. Dependabot opens PRs that update dependencies; CI then tells you whether the update is safe to merge. It understands uv.lock and your workflow files:

.github/dependabot.yml:

version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: "uv"
    directory: "/"
    schedule: {interval: "weekly"}
    groups:                       # one PR for all minor/patch updates
      minor-and-patch:
        update-types: ["minor", "patch"]
  - package-ecosystem: "github-actions"   # bumps actions/checkout@v7 ...
    directory: "/"
    schedule: {interval: "monthly"}

This is where your test suite pays off a second time: a good suite lets you merge a "bump scikit-learn" PR in one minute. Without one, nobody dares, and the project ages until an upgrade becomes a project of its own.

GitHub Actions is free for public repositories. For private ones, GitHub Free includes 2,000 Linux minutes per month (check the current plan details), and wasted minutes add up quickly in a team. The levers:

  • Concurrency groups. concurrency: group: ci-${{ github.ref }} with

cancel-in-progress: true cancels the still-running pipeline of a PR when you push a new commit: nobody needs the result for an outdated commit. Our file only cancels on PRs; runs on main always finish.

• Path filters. paths: / paths-ignore: skip workflows when irrelevant files change (docs, README). Careful: a required check that is skipped by a path filter can block merging. Either keep required workflows unfiltered or filter at the job level.
  • Job dependencies. Cheap jobs first (lint takes 15 seconds), expensive ones only if those pass (needs:).
  • Caching and timeouts, as above.
  • Right-size the matrix. Test all versions on PRs to main, but not necessarily all operating systems; nightly runs can cover the rest.

Everything so far fits one repository and one person. In a team of thirty with a dozen models, the questions change from "how do I write a test?" to "which tests run where, how long may they take, and who owns them?". A senior engineer can draw this on a whiteboard:

LayerExamples in this bookBudgetRuns on
Static checksruff, mypy, actionlint, secret scan< 1 minevery push
Unit teststest_gate.py, behavioural tests with a tiny model< 3 minevery push
Data and modeldata contract, train on a sample, metric gate< 10 minevery PR
Integrationpgvector test, API against a real database< 10 minPR (paths) and main
Full evaluationfull-data training, LLM faithfulness, slices< 60 minmain, nightly
Post-deploysmoke test, distribution check, load test< 10 minafter each deploy

The budgets are the point: a layer that exceeds its budget moves down a row (runs less often) or gets faster. Four practices keep this working in a team:

  • Contract tests between services. When another team calls

/predict, write down what they rely on (fields, types, status codes) as a test that runs in your CI. Tools such as Pact automate this between repositories; a JSON schema checked in both repos is the lightweight version. It turns "expand, then contract" (Chapter 5) from a promise into a check.

• A load test with a gate. A short k6 or Locust run against staging that fails if p95 latency exceeds the SLO (Chapter 7). Ten minutes of load after deploy catches the memory leak and the missing index that unit tests never will.
  • A flaky-test policy. A test that fails without a code change gets a

flaky label, an owner and a deadline; it is quarantined (skipped in the required check, still run and reported elsewhere) until fixed. Without a policy, "re-run until green" becomes the culture and the required check means nothing.

  • Ownership. CODEOWNERS makes the right people review changes to thresholds, evaluation sets, infrastructure and workflows. In

credit-api, .github/CODEOWNERS assigns metrics/, gate.py, infra/ and the workflows; combined with the ruleset option Require review from Code Owners, nobody lowers a quality gate without the owner's approval.

Interview tip

"I'd draw the test pyramid with a time budget per layer, and enforce the budgets: if the unit tests take longer than three minutes, that is a bug. Contract tests protect our consumers, a short load test protects the SLO, and flaky tests get quarantined with an owner, never re-run until green."

Exercise: Add an OS dimension

Extend the matrix to run the tests on ubuntu-latest and macos-latest for Python 3.12 only, using include:. How many jobs run now? Why might macOS minutes be more expensive on private repositories?

Exercise: Protect yourself

Create the ruleset described above on your credit-api repository. Then open a PR that breaks ruff format --check and confirm that GitHub refuses to merge it.

Exercise: Prove the aggregator

With ci-ok as the only required check, (a) change the matrix to ["3.13", "3.14"] and confirm the PR can still be merged, and (b) remove if: always() from ci-ok, break a test, and look at what ci-ok reports. Why is (b) dangerous?

Exercise: Read the linters

Copy features.py from this chapter into credit-api/src/credit_api/, run ruff and mypy, and fix every finding by hand (no --fix). Which fix changes the behaviour of the code?

Checkpoint: you should now be able to…

• run ruff, mypy and pytest locally and via pre-commit;
  • explain the bugs behind B006 and mypy's [return] error, and introduce linters into a legacy codebase step by step;
  • require one aggregator check instead of matrix job names, and explain merge queues and merge_group;
  • recognise the pull_request_target trap and unmasked transformed secrets;
  • explain caching, matrix builds and the coverage threshold;
  • make checks required with a branch ruleset and merge a PR end to end;
  • store and use secrets and variables, and react to a leaked key;
  • reduce CI time and cost with concurrency, path filters, needs and timeouts.
